newsitem.title: ITALY: Mafioso says Italy's Andreotti was close to Mob.
newsitem.headline: Mafioso says Italy's Andreotti was close to Mob.

text.p: One of the Mafia's leading bosses, Giovanni Brusca, told a court on Monday that former Italian prime minister Giulio Andreotti helped the Mob to fix trials.

Brusca, 32, testifying in public for the first time since his arrest last May, was at a trial in Rome where he and other arrested Mafiosi, including "boss of bosses" Salvatore Riina, are accused of murder.
"When I heard we were in a position to intervene at the level of Andreotti to fix trials, and my father and others confirmed that, I felt important," Brusca said.
Andreotti, who was prime minister seven times, has been on trial since late 1994 on charges that he was the Mafia's chief political protector for more than a decade.
The 78-year-old life senator denies allegations that he helped fix trials and obtain other favours for the Mafia in return for support in Sicily.
Brusca has been cooperating with the authorities since his arrest but investigators have doubts about his sincerity.
He has not been given access to Italy's witness protection scheme while anti-Mafia magistrates decide whether he is a "fake turncoat" who has been deliberately trying to mislead them.
His testimony about his life in the Mafia followed newspaper reports that his brother Enzo, who was arrested with him, had also spoken of Andreotti's alleged links to crime.
The reports said Enzo had told investigators he was sure that Andreotti had kissed Riina at an alleged meeting in 1987.
"My brother Emanuele (another Mafioso) told me that my father Bernardo knew Andreotti kissed Riina," the reports said.
Allegations by Riina's former bodyguard Balduccio Di Maggio that the two met and kissed, denied by Andreotti, form part of the prosecution evidence at the former prime minister's trial.
Prosecutors allege that Giovanni Brusca was one of the most bloodthirsty Mafia leaders and the Mob's effective "military chief".
He is accused among other crimes of detonating a bomb which blew up star anti-Mafia magistrate Giovanni Falcone, his wife and three bodyguards on a motorway near Palermo in 1992.
Riina and other defendants listened impassively in court as Brusca gave his testimony.
"I became a Mafioso in 1977 or 1978. I was only a foot soldier but I was Bernardo's son and Riina was my godfather," Brusca said.
"Because of that I was considered more than other people and I worked very closely with Riina especially (in dealings) with the Salvo cousins," Brusca added.
The Salvos, who are both dead, were tax collectors in Sicily with close ties to the Mafia.
